description: Unlocking Institutional Borrowing and Lending Rates With Box Spreads
body_html:

  1. Introduction

  2. What are Box Spreads / Portfolio Margin

  3. Uncertain Taxation of Box Spreads and the BOXX ETF

  4. Using Box Spreads to Borrow and Lend at Favorable Rates

  5. Risks

  6. Conclusion

1. Introduction

Box Spreads seem to have earned a mythical reputation recently. We hear constant whispers of tax advantages and attractive funding rates, yet concrete examples remain elusive.

(Pictured Above: Bloomberg Article on the BOXX ETF)

With ETFs such as BOXX (that employ Box Spreads to generate money market like returns) soaring in popularity, I wanted to write a brief piece on what SPX Box Spreads are, the uncertain taxation risks associated with Box Spreads and the BOXX ETF, and show a real life example of borrowing and lending $100,000 near the Overnight Bank Funding Rate (currently 3.64%) via SPX Box Spreads.

While Box Spreads enable market participants to borrow and lend to each other at highly favorable rates (currently 3.94% for lending, 4.07% for borrowing), it’d be remiss to ignore the fact tax treatment of Box Spreads and the BOXX ETF is uncertain.

There is considerable debate over whether Section 1258 of the Tax Code applies to income generated from loans facilitated by Section 1256 Box Spreads, and the future of current BOXX “loophole” may close - the IRS may one day issue a notice requiring BOXX profits to be reclassified as Interest Income, forcing investors to refile previous taxes and creating significant adverse tax consequences (here is an excellent article explaining that risk). There’s no such thing as a free-lunch.

Since I am not a Tax Professional, I am not taking a position on potential tax treatment - I will simply discuss what both sides argue. The tax implications of Box Spreads and the BOXX ETF is a matter for you and your qualified Tax Professionals to determine.

Additionally, the utilization of Portfolio Margin to borrow or lend via Box Spreads involves the use of advanced margin calculations and significant financial risk. Portfolio Margin is designed for experienced, sophisticated investors who fully understand the risks of leveraged trading and may result in rapid, substantial losses in excess of your account’s equity. Whether Box Spread borrowing and Portfolio Margin is appropriate for you is a matter for you to decide in consultation with qualified Tax and Financial Advisors.

2. What are Box Spreads / Portfolio Margin

A Box Spread is a 4-legged options combination that combines a Bull Call Spread (long lower strike Call, short higher strike Call) and a Bear Put Spread (long higher strike Put, short lower strike Put) at the same strikes. When conducted with European-Style Index Options (such as SPX Index Options that cannot be exercised early) a Box Spread generates a fixed payout upon maturity: no matter where the index settles, the Bull Call Spread and Bear Put Spread offset and the final value of the combination is always equal to the width of the strikes.

Given the fixed payout, Box Spreads on European-Style Index Options offer market participants a way to borrow and lend funds to each other at attractive rates. All US Options Trades are guaranteed by the Options Clearing Corporation (AA rated), the Central Counterparty to all US Options Trades, as a result counterparty risk is minimal since repayment is guaranteed by the OCC.

The price of an SPX Box Spread today is merely a future payout discounted by an implied interest rate. It is a time-value-of-money calculation in the purest sense.

Here is an illustration. Imagine you are a market participant looking to lend out $100,000. You can purchase a SPX 6000 - 7000 Box Spread, and receive a $100,000 Payout (1,000 strike width x $100 a contract multiplier) upon maturity:

Long 1x SPX 6000-7000 Box Spread (Lending):

  • Long the Bull Call Spread

    • Buy 1x 6000 Call

    • Sell 1x 7000 Call

  • Long the Bear Put Spread

    • Buy 1x 7000 Put

    • Sell 1x 6000 Put

As you can see, no matter where the index settles the combined value of the 4 legs is 1,000 at expiration (the width of the Box).

Imagine this hypothetical Box Spread has an expiry in exactly 90 days. What should the price be today? The value of the Box Spread today is simply the interest rate you discount that future payout by.

Imagine your implied interest rate is 4%:

Future Payout = $100,000 (1,000 strike width x $100 multiplier)

Present Value = Future Payout / ((1 + Interest Rate) ^ (Days to Maturity / 365))

Present Value = $100,000 / ((1 + 0.04) ^ (90 / 365))

Present Value = $100,000 / (1.04^0.2645753)

Present Value = $99,037

Price of Box Spread = $99,037 / 100 a contract = $990.37

The price you would pay for this Box Spread is $990.37, and in 90 days the Box Spread would settle for $1,000, implying an interest rate of 4%.

When calculating the implied interest rate on a Box Spread, there are several compounding conventions you could apply. Traditional markets often use 30 / 360 (assuming 30-day months and a 360-day year) or actual / 360, which is common in money markets and Short-Term lending. I've chosen to use actual / 365 with daily compounding, because it most accurately reflects the annualized cost of borrowing and provides a cleaner comparison to margin rates and Treasury yields.

Now, let’s say you want to borrow $100,000, rather than lend.

You simply construct the Box Spread with the direction of each leg flipped. This time you are are shorting a Bull Call Spread and a Bear Put Spread, instead of buying them.

Short 1x SPX 6000-7000 Box Spread (Borrowing):

  • Short Bull Call Spread

    • Sell 1x 6000 Call

    • Buy 1x 7000 Call

  • Short Bear Put Spread

    • Sell 1x 7000 Put

    • Buy 1x 6000 Put

In this instance, you are receiving cash upfront, and upon maturity you will have to return $1,000 (x 100 multiplier), no matter where the index settles.

The price of this spread, at an implied interest rate of 4%, would be -990.37, meaning that you are borrowing 990.37 x 100 today, and the combination would settle at -1,000, meaning you have to return 1000 x 100 upon expiration.

Hopefully these examples illustrate how SPX Box Spreads are time value of money instruments - you either borrow or lend today, and repay when the Box Spread expires.

The implied interest rates of SPX Box Spreads tend to track the Overnight Bank Funding Rate closely. In general, you can borrow via Box Spreads around 35-45 bps higher than the OBFR, and lend via Box Spreads at 20-25 bps higher than the OBFR. Naturally, Box Spreads offer rates at a small premium to Treasuries, as the OCC is slightly less creditworthy than the US Treasury. Hundreds of Millions of dollars are regularly borrowed and lent via market participants through SPX Box Spreads, and you can monitor recent transactions and rates at Box Trades.

Box Spreads for borrowing and lending are only capital efficient if you have Portfolio Margin.

Portfolio Margin is an advanced margin methodology for highly experienced traders that calculates collateral requirements based on the overall risk of your portfolio, rather than each individual position. If you hold offsetting positions, such 4 legs belonging to a Box Spread, Portfolio Margin recognizes this and requires significantly less collateral. Regulation T margin, in contrast, evaluates each leg in isolation and demands far more capital.

As a result, Regulation T margin ties up so much capital with Box Spreads you can’t utilize the cash you borrow, making borrowing a useless endeavor. If you chose to lend via Box Spreads in a normal margin account, the requirements are somewhat similar to selling cash secured puts - that capital is tied up and unable to be used until you close your position out - making it highly unfavorable.

While brokers often offer Portfolio Margin if you have more than $125,000 in Equity, you shouldn’t even consider Portfolio Margin unless you have extensive trading experience, equity significantly higher than required minimums, and have consulted qualified advisors.

Box Spread borrowing is an advanced tactic that is complex to implement, and if you attempt Box Spread borrowing with insufficient equity and dip below your broker’s Portfolio Margin minimum, your account may immediately revert to Regulation T margin rules. This leads to a higher margin requirement on your Box Spreads, and can result in a catastrophic, immediate, margin call. Box Spreads and Portfolio Margin are not trivial matters.

Now that we have discussed what Box Spreads are, and the risks associated with Portfolio Margin, I want to briefly discuss the uncertain Taxation of Box Spreads and the BOXX ETF before jumping into a implementation.

3. Uncertain Taxation of Box Spreads and the BOXX ETF

The Taxation of Box Spreads is uncertain.

SPX Options, in general, qualify for preferential Section 1256 Treatment.

Section 1256 contracts receive preferential tax treatment where gains and losses are marked-to-market at year-end and taxed using a 60/40 blended rate: 60% Long-Term Capital Gains, 40% Short-Term Capital Gains regardless of how long you held the position. This effectively caps your maximum federal rate around 26.8% (plus a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax) instead of the 37% (plus a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax) Short-Term rate.

This preferential treatment applies to regulated futures contracts (Index Futures, Precious Metals Futures, Energy Futures), broad-based index options (SPX, NDX, RUT) and certain foreign currency contracts. Losses on Section 1256 products can also be carried back 3 years against prior Section 1256 gains, a unique benefit. It may seem ridiculous that these financial derivatives qualify for 60% Long-Term Capital Gains treatment regardless of how long they are held, but I don’t write the rules.

(On an unrelated note, if you are an avid trader of SPY or SPY Options, you can significantly lower your tax bill by trading ES Futures or SPX Index Options provided you are a highly experienced investor and comfortable with these products)

As a result of Section 1256, you would assume interest-like income from Box Spreads would be eligible for preferential Section 1256 Treatment, allowing you a magical method to convert what might be highly taxed Interest Income (from bank accounts or broker’s cash sweeps) into more favorably taxed Section 1256 Income (and slash your tax bill from 40.8% to 26.8%).

Not so fast.

Section 1258 of the tax code was designed to prevent this type of maneuvering. Section 1258 recharacterizes capital gains as ordinary income on "conversion transactions" where substantially all of the expected return is attributable to the time value of money, and the taxpayer has diminished risk of loss through offsetting positions.

Let’s be honest with ourselves here, this is pretty much the exact definition of a Box Spread.

The economic return of a Box Spread is purely derived from the time value of money, and the substance of the transaction is almost indistinguishable for lending or borrowing cash.

Nonetheless, brokers by default report gains and losses derived from Box Spreads in the Section 1256 part of your 1099, and investors have reported it as such and gotten away with it.

Proponents of reporting Box Spread gains and losses this way argue Section 1256 explicitly names broad-based index options as covered contracts with no carve-out, even if you are using them in Box Spreads, and additionally, point to the fact the IRS has never (at least to anyone’s knowledge) issued a clarification as to whether Box Spread income or expense should be reclassified under Section 1258 as Interest Income or Interest Expense.

The real argument in favor of Section 1256 Treatment can be summarized by: “It’s probably bending the law by reporting it this way, but no one has told us explicitly we can’t do this”.

As a result, is the “Interest Income” received from Box Spread purchases Section 1256 Eligible? Should the “Interest Expense” associated with Box Spread borrowing be reported as a Section 1256 Loss or an Investment Interest Expense? Unfortunately, no one really knows the answer until the IRS definitely says so.

The BOXX ETF invests primarily in SPX Box Spreads (and has reported income from its one distribution as Section 1256 Income). Assets within the BOXX ETF have soared to a jaw-dropping $9.62 Billion, and the ETF counts several Wealth Management Firms as top holders. Why? BOXX takes Box Spreads a step further.

(Pictured Below: BOXX Shares Outstanding in thousands)

(Pictured Below: Top Holders of BOXX)

How?

The prospect of Tax Deferral.

Bloomberg has an excellent writeup on BOXX’s advanced deferral mechanics: it uses complex financial engineering to avoid having to pay out distributions.

BOXX invests in Box Spreads (that generate money-market like returns), but its advanced financial engineering prevents distributions from being made, enabling capital to grow without generating tax bills until you sell (unless the IRS decides to stop this). Generally, ETFs distribute dividends and realized capital gains, resulting in taxable events for its holders. But with no distributions, there are no taxable events.

Since inception, BOXX has made only one distribution on August 13, 2024 (they characterized the SPX Box Spread income as Section 1256 Income when distributed - 60% Long-Term, 40% Short-Term) and have since avoided making distributions. Not only has this allowed investor’s principal to grow tax deferred, but investors who hold the ETF for a year before selling have claimed Long-Term Capital Gains treatment on their entire profit, effectively converting what is an interest-like return (which could be taxed as high as 40.8% at the Federal level) entirely into Long-Term Capital Gains (taxed at just 23.8%).

This “loophole” has heavily benefited High Net Worth residents of high tax states who who intend to move to lower tax jurisdictions.

Take, for example, a mega rich New Yorker who carries $10 Million in cash. He (or she) might’ve invested the $10 Million in BOXX in 2023, moved to Texas in early 2026, and sold the entire position. By not receiving a distribution in 2023, 2024, and 2025, they have no state tax liability for those years. Once they become a Texas resident, they can sell their entire position without ever paying state taxes. In essence, BOXX has been used by many as a tool to defer Federal taxes, and dodge state taxes, on cash you intend to lock up for a while. (It is important to note you can also avoid State and Local Taxes by leaving spare cash in Treasury Bills).

It seems like an incredible loophole to defer Federal and State taxes, but Daniel J. Hemel, professor of Tax Law at New York University, explains why this “loophole” may actually blow up in everyone’s face.

Hemel states the IRS has multiple options to crack down on this deferral.

First of all, they could clarify Box Spread income is, in fact, Interest Income that is ineligible for Section 1256 Treatment, impacting raw Box Spread lenders and classifying BOXX’s Box Spread profits as Interest Income. If this occurs, it’s possible the IRS makes the clarification retroactive to previous tax returns, forcing anyone who declared Box Spread income as Section 1256 Income to refile tax returns for periods up to 6 years prior. Additionally, Box Spread borrowers who reported the expense associated with Box Spreads as a Section 1256 Loss would need to reclassify these losses as Investment Interest Expense.

Secondly, the IRS could crackdown on BOXX’s innovative deferral mechanism, forcing the fund to pay out any income. A distribution of income triggers a taxable event, and adverse tax consequences for Long-Term BOXX holders who bought it with the intent of deferring income.

Lastly, the IRS could go nuclear, declaring BOXX itself a Section 1258 “Conversion Transaction”, potentially forcing taxpayers who previously sold their shares for Long-Term Capital Gains profits to reclassify these profits at Interest Income, if the IRS chooses to make this effective retroactively. This could result in ETF holders needing to restate several years of returns, and reclassifying previous Realized Long-Term Capital Gains as much more highly taxed Interest Income.

As you can see, the Tax Treatment of Box Spreads and BOXX is anything but certain. Is lending income from Box Spreads Section 1256 Eligible? Will the BOXX deferral mechanism persist? Uncertain.

On the flip side, we have the ex-Mayor of New York City promoting a memecoin, a seemingly thriving Somalian childcare sector in Minnesota, and the President’s own Social Media Network merging with a pre-revenue Nuclear Fusion Company.

If there is one thing I am sure of, it’s that regulators have plenty of things to go after.

The bottom line is - Box Spreads and BOXX may offer innovative tax benefits (wealth management firms certainly seem to think so), but an adverse IRS ruling could trigger tax bills and refiling needs. Proceed with caution and consult an experienced Tax Attorney to fully understand the tax implications of Box Spreads.

4. Using Box Spreads to Borrow and Lend at Favorable Rates

Now that we have a small foundation on what SPX Box Spreads are, and the uncertain tax treatment associated with them, let’s get into a real world example of borrowing and lending cash.

Before making a loan or borrowing cash, we need to determine:

  1. Expiry Selection

  2. Width Selection

  3. Compute Effective Interest Rate

  4. Verify and Execute

Expiry Selection and Width Selection

First, you need to select a SPX expiry. The expiration date of your Box Spread determines the length of your loan. If you want to borrow or lend for 3 months, select an SPX expiration approximately 3 months out. If you want a 1-year term, select an SPX expiration approximately 1 year out.

A few guidelines for determining expiration:

  • Stick to 12 months or shorter: Liquidity deteriorates on longer-dated options past 12 months, resulting in wider spreads and poor execution. If you are looking to borrow cash for 3+ years, you will have to use shorter dated spreads and roll them

  • Use monthly AM-settled SPX expirations: These are the most liquid and have the tightest spreads. Avoid weekly expirations.

  • Execute during regular market hours: Liquidity is almost non-existent outside normal market hours, and in fact, the complex order book may be closed. Only execute between 10 AM EST and 3 PM EST

  • Keep Strike Width below $1,000: A strike width of $1,000 implies you are borrowing or lending $100,000 ($1,000 x 100 a contract). If you attempt to execute a Box Spread wider than 1,000 points in width, you may encounter difficulties in execution. It’s best to keep the Maximum Strike Width at 1,000, if you need to borrow a larger amount than $100,000, you can execute several 1,000 point wide Box Spreads.

  • Submit all four legs as a single complex order: Do not attempt to execute the legs individually.

I can’t stress the last point enough. A Box Spread is a 4-legged trade, and is meant to be executed as a “complex order”. If you attempt to fill legs on an individual basis, you will receive inferior execution, open yourself up to market risk as the index moves during execution, and lastly, you may make an implementation mistake. Do not execute legs individually.

Computing the Effective Interest Rate

The Effective Interest Rate formula is computed by:

(Amount Returned / Amount Borrowed) ^ (365 / Days) - 1 = Effective Interest Rate

Days: US Options settle T+1. This means if you purchase a Box Spread on Monday, the cash doesn’t actually settle in your account until Tuesday. For SPX AM Monthly Options, trading typically stops Thursday but the options actually expire at the open on Friday, and final cash settlement occurs the following Monday (T+1). Make sure you have your Settlement dates written down, and you can use Excel to determine the Days of the Loan (difference between Settlement Dates), by subtracting them in Excel.

Now, let’s run through two real life examples of borrowing and lending. I conducted these trades on December 19th, 2025 (so while it is spoken in present tense, keep in mind these rates are about a month old, and I made this trade on Friday, December 19th).

Example 1: Borrowing $100,000 for 3 Months

Step 1: Expiry Selection

First, navigate to Option Chain for SPX on IBKR and find the closest AM-settled monthly expiration matching our desired term. The March 19, 2026 AM expiration fits the criteria and is almost exactly 3 months out.

Our expiry will be the March 19, 2026 SPX Monthly AM expiration. Keep in mind the expiration date for AM settled options is almost always the Friday after, so the options expire on March 20th, 2026, and the cash will settle in our account on Monday March 23rd, 2026. Since today is Friday, December 19, 2025, the cash will settle in our account T+1 (Monday, December 22, 2025), so the length of the loan is 03/23/2026 - 12/22/2025 = 91 days

Step 2: Strike Selection

Since we want to borrow $100,000, we need a 1,000-point-wide box (1,000 points × $100 multiplier = $100,000 at expiration). With SPX trading around 6,800, we select 6,300 for our lower strike and 7,300 for our upper strike, so the index is directly in the middle

Step 3: Compute the Effective Interest Rate

As we recall, the structure for borrowing (selling a Box) is to short a Bull Call Spread and Short a Bear Put Spread

  • Sell Bull Call Spread

    • Sell 1x March 2026 SPX 6,300 Call

    • Buy 1x March 2026 SPX 7,300 Call

  • Sell Bear Put Spread

    • Sell a March 2026 SPX 7,300 Put

    • Buy a March 2026 SPX 6,300 Put

We can create this in IBKR by using the Option Chain, enabling the strategy builder, and selecting our strikes (click the bid of the March 2026 SPX 6,300 Call to add it as a sell, the ask of the March 2026 SPX 7,300 Call to add it as buy, etc).

(the … below Type should be Call, but it was compressed by the window)

Once constructed, Strategy Builder should show a credit, which this confirms you are borrowing, and should list the combination as a “Box”. If it does not list it as a Box, you have not constructed it properly.

The midpoint of the spread is -989.30, meaning we receive $98,930 in cash upfront (settling Monday, December 22) and repay $100,000 in cash at expiration (settling March 23).

Now, we Compute the Effective Interest Rate

(Amount Returned / Amount Borrowed) ^ (365 / Days) - 1 = Effective Interest Rate

($100,000 / $98,930) ^ (365 / 91) - 1 = 4.41%

This means, at the midpoint, we are borrowing $98,930 (989.30 Credit x 100) at 4.41% for 91 days. This rate is a bit higher than we would expect, but given interest rates have just been cut, it may take the Box Spread market a day or two to adjust.

It is best practice to start an order at a bid (implying a better interest rate) and work your way up to the mid, but for this trade I decided to just submit at the mid.

We hit the Submit Order button, and the Order Confirmation window displays the “SPX Box” within the Order Description, and shows a Credit (Green C) as the Amount. We have constructed the Box properly.

The order fills instantly.

Given how quickly it filled, it means we probably left cash on the table and could’ve filled at -989.35 or even -989.40 (borrowing more cash and paying a lower interest rate).

Example: Lending $100,000 for 3 Months

For this example, I am skipping Step 1 and Step 2, since we are going to use the exact same expiration and strikes to lend.

Step 3: Compute the Effective Interest Rate

As we recall, the structure for lending (buying a Box) is to buy a Bull Call Spread and buy a Bear Put Spread

  • Long Bull Call Spread

    • Buy 1x March 2026 SPX 6,300 Call

    • Sell 1x March 2026 SPX 7,300 Call

  • Long Bear Put Spread

    • Buy a March 2026 SPX 7,300 Put

    • Sell a March 2026 SPX 6,300 Put

We create this on the IBKR Option Chain, and see the following:

(the … below Type should be Call, but it was compressed by the window)

The Strategy Builder displays a debit (confirming we are lending cash) and the margin requirement is once again minimal, indicating we formed the Box Correctly.

The midpoint is now 989.00, so we calculate the effective interest rate.

(Amount Returned / Amount Borrowed) ^ (365 / Days) - 1 = Effective Interest Rate

($100,000 / $98,900) ^ (365 / 91) - 1 = 4.54%

Given we just borrowed cash at 4.41%, it is unlikely we can lend at a higher rate, but for the purposes of this example I start at the midpoint.

The Order Confirmation once again confirms we are trading a box, and the Red D confirms it is a debit (loan).

This time there is no instant fill, because the market makers aren’t willing to borrow at 4.54%. We inch our order towards the ask, meaning we lend out more cash and receive less interest (a lower implied interest rate)

989.05

989.10

989.15

…

989.85. We fill.

Let’s open Excel up again.

The effective interest rate is 4.18%

($100,000 / $98,985) ^ (365 / 91) - 1 = 4.18%

We borrowed cash via Box Spreads at 4.41%, and lent cash at 4.18%. The spread between borrowing at 989.30 (4.41%) and lending at 989.85 (4.18%) is just 23 basis points, extremely tight.

As you can see, the rates via Box Spread lending and borrowing are significantly superior to cash interest and margin rates offered by even the most competitive brokers.

As of today, January 14th, Box Spread rates have dropped further, to roughly 3.94% if you want to lend, and 4.12% if you want to borrow, on the February 19th AM Settled SPX Expiration.

The beauty of these competitive interest rates is that they come without negotiation. At most brokers, you need to carry a sizeable balances to qualify for competitive margin rates.

Box borrowing and lending rates, on the other hand, come without negotiation and are accessible even if you are looking to borrow or lend a small amount.

Even Interactive Broker’s most competitive margin rate (4.14% on Margin Balances in excess of $50,000,000) and cash rate (3.14% on Balances in excess of $10,000), can’t come close.

The bottom line is, if you are an experienced investor with Portfolio Margin capabilities and sizeable margin or cash balances, you may be able to optimize rates on spare cash or borrowings, provided you are willing to accept the uncertain tax treatment associated with Box Spreads.

5. Risks

Trading on margin or using Box Spreads involves borrowed funds. The use of borrowed funds creates the risk of losses in excess of your account equity.

Portfolio Margin permits substantially higher leverage than standard margin accounts by calculating margin requirements based on the overall risk of a portfolio rather than individual positions. Portfolio Margin accounts are intended for sophisticated investors with significant experience, and are highly unsuitable for most investors.

Box Spreads carry counterparty risk relative to Treasuries. While the OCC is an AA rated institution, a sudden collapse of the US Financial System could potentially render the OCC insolvent. While this outcome is possible, it is unlikely because a collapse of the OCC likely occurs alongside a collapse of the overall system (FDIC, SIPC, Banks, Brokers), making money equivalent to toilet paper. Private Credit which will naturally be fine (I’m kidding).

Frankly, the main risk when trading Box Spreads is implementation error: entering an order incorrectly or getting filled at a horrible price.

This is why double and triple checking the order placement screen is a must.

  • Never submit market orders

  • Never submit legs individually

  • Trade during liquid market hours (10 AM to 3 PM EST) where conditions are calm

  • Triple check you have formed a Box Spread correctly (most advanced brokerage platforms will identify the combination as Box)

  • Compute the Effective Interest Rate via calculator and Excel, and run a sanity check (“I’m borrowing 96,000 today and returning 100,000 in 12 months, this seems about right”)

  • Continue computing the Effective Interest Rate as you move your order to ensure you are still trading at a reasonable implied rate

  • For best execution, start your order on the optimal side (borrowing more if you are a borrower - which means a higher credit, lending less if you are a lender - a lower debit), and slowly moving your order towards the midpoint

6. Conclusion

Box Spreads provide an effective way to borrow and lend near benchmark interest rates, provided you have ample capital, appropriate Portfolio Margin permissions, and are an experienced trader.

While Box Spreads provide an attractive avenue to borrow and lend at superior interest rates, the Tax Treatment of Box Spreads and BOXX is highly uncertain.

Future IRS rulings could severely impact your tax liability and result in you needing to refile taxes for previous periods if you borrow or lend via Box Spreads.

Additionally, the “Interest Expense” associated with Box Spread borrowing may not be fully deductible if you lack capital gains - you should consult experienced Tax Advisors, Tax Attorneys, and Financial Planners to ascertain the Tax and Financial ramifications of Box Spreads and BOXX, and to determine if Portfolio Margin is suitable for your risk appetite, prior to making any type of financial decision.

I know this has been a lengthy piece. Hopefully, you now have a solid handle on what Box Spreads are and how they can be used.
